articles.title_orig: China Export Controls: Interim Tech Registration
articles.title_zh: China Export Controls: Interim Tech Registration
articles.content_orig:
Editorial · CASRAI · Compliance and regulatory
China enforces interim pre-export registration on 40 emerging AI, photovoltaic, and biotech technologies following the close of public consultation.
Following the November 15, 2026 close of public consultation on Announcement [2026] No. 48, China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology are enforcing immediate interim pre-export registration across 40 technologies proposed for addition to the national export-control catalogue, compelling international research universities, cross-border joint institutes, and technology-transfer offices to audit outbound data transfers and collaborative intellectual property arrangements.
The regulatory transition, initiated formally on November 16, 2026, marks the operational shift from public notice to active administrative gatekeeping. Jointly promulgated by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) Bureau of Industry Security and Export Control and the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) under Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, the initiative updates the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. While formal Catalogue additions were open for public comment through mid-November, Chinese trade authorities enacted a mandatory pre-export filing obligation that took immediate effect upon publication.
The 40 targeted technologies expand oversight across three strategic domains. Regulators divided the technologies into two legal tiers: 14 technologies are prohibited from export, imposing an absolute ban on cross-border transfer, while 26 technologies are restricted from export, requiring administrative licensing reviews.
Artificial intelligence accounts for 23 of the 40 items, targeting foundation model parameters, large language model weights, autonomous agent architectures, intelligent computing clusters, and automated vulnerability discovery tools. The remaining items cover 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies—focusing on polysilicon crystallization, wafer slicing, and high-efficiency solar cells—and 5 biomanufacturing technologies encompassing cell and gene therapies, small nucleic acid platforms, and pathogen genetic modification methods.
The regulatory schedule establishes concrete technical thresholds to distinguish between prohibited systems, restricted technologies subject to licensing, and unencumbered commercial activities.
For large language models, restricted status applies when a model satisfies any of three quantitative tests: training compute reaching or exceeding 10²⁶ floating-point operations (FLOPs), total model parameters reaching or exceeding 2 trillion, or global top-10 performance on recognized public benchmarks. When a model crosses these thresholds, restrictions attach to model weights, training checkpoints, architecture design documents, and optimization know-how.
Crucially, the rules establish explicit carve-outs. Technologies that have entered the public domain through open-source repository releases or published peer-reviewed academic literature are expressly excluded. Furthermore, MOFCOM clarified that providing foreign end-users with remote access to models hosted on domestic Chinese servers via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) portals, mobile applications, or lightweight on-device runtimes does not constitute a technology export. An export occurs only when model weights, code, or custodial infrastructure are physically transferred or deployed on foreign infrastructure.
In biomanufacturing, authorities introduced a distinction between platform ownership and product-specific licensing. The export prohibition applies exclusively to outbound assignments of intellectual property ownership over reusable foundational platforms. Cross-border out-licensing agreements involving specific therapeutic drug candidates remain eligible for streamlined administrative reviews and prospective automatic licensing, provided that underlying platform intellectual property remains domiciled in China.
The enforcement of Announcement [2026] No. 48 represents the most substantial structural revision to China’s technology export controls since August 2020. China maintains two parallel statutory frameworks governing cross-border transfers. The dual-use export control regime, administered under the Export Control Law of 2020, governs tangible items, software, and technical data with dual civilian and military utility. In contrast, the technology-trade regime, established under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, regulates commercial transfers of intellectual property, proprietary know-how, and industrial contracts.
The Catalogue was established in 2001 and revised in 2008 and 2020. The 2020 amendments added personalized recommendation algorithms and speech synthesis. The 2026 revisions expand this conceptual foundation to foundational compute infrastructure, synthetic biology platforms, and renewable energy manufacturing.
International regulatory divergence forms the broader context for these measures. As Western jurisdictions expand export controls through instruments such as the United States Export Control Reform Act , semiconductor equipment restrictions, and outbound investment screening, Chinese authorities have modernized their legal architecture. The November 2026 interim measures establish a statutory perimeter designed to prevent the unauthorized transfer of critical technological capabilities developed with domestic funding or proprietary subsidies.
International trade counsel and industry research bodies have evaluated institutional exposure under the interim rules. Legal practitioners at Baker McKenzie observed that immediate interim registration creates an enforceable compliance obligation before the final Catalogue is codified into law. Trade attorneys noted that while registration does not constitute formal export approval, failure to complete pre-export filings before transferring controlled code, data, or technical assistance exposes institutions to administrative penalties under Chinese foreign trade law.
Technical governance analysts at the Cloud Security Alliance highlighted the sophistication of the quantitative criteria, noting that compute thresholds at 10²⁶ FLOPs align with international safety evaluation benchmarks. The organization stressed that separating API-based service access from localized model weight deployments offers vital operational clarity, allowing multinational software ecosystems to operate across Chinese borders so long as model custody remains inside domestic server facilities.
In life sciences, legal specialists at Morgan Lewis emphasized that multinational pharmaceutical developers must conduct immediate portfolio reviews. Corporate acquirers and licensees were advised to structure licensing transactions as product-specific grants rather than platform acquisitions, ensuring that deal documents explicitly separate specific drug candidates from reusable screening platforms to avoid triggering mandatory export prohibitions.
Cross-border investment advisors at Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman warned that interim registration reaches beyond conventional technology sales. The firm highlighted that corporate mergers, equity acquisitions, or corporate restructuring transactions that result in a foreign entity acquiring actual control over a domestic Chinese entity holding controlled technologies constitute an export event requiring pre-closing registration with provincial commerce bureaus.
The enforcement of interim registration imposes direct compliance obligations on international higher education institutions, Sino-foreign cooperative universities, and academic research centres. articles.title_orig: China Spring Park is open to the public
articles.title_zh: China Spring Park is open to the public
articles.content_orig:
Hi! I'm Chantale Belefanti, your Neighborhood Reporter for China Spring, Hillsboro, and Valley Mills.
CHINA SPRING, Texas (KXXV) — China Spring Park is now open to the public. Several China Spring neighbors said they’re happy to have a park with a lot of features finally.
“I feel like it’s well built and it has a lot of activities," said Melana Webb, an 11-year-old from China Spring.
Webb and her friends have a park to go to in China Spring, and it’s new.
“There are some parts in our neighborhoods that we can play on, but they’re not fun like this… this is amazing. This is something I would want to come to a lot," said Webb.
The almost 90-acre park located off Flat Rock Drive features a splash pad, playground, basketball court, trail, bathrooms, and more.
The City of Waco Mayor Jim Holmes and city officials opened the approximately $8 million dollar park with a ribbon-cutting. Mayor Holmes said the park is very much needed.
“This community has needed a park for some time, and it’s sort of a park desert in this part of the city, so opening this kind of park, and this kind of space and amenities is just super,"  Holmes said.
“The trail over there feels like you’re playing Mario Kart but in real life," said Adrian Andrade of China Spring.
And the best part about it is that it’s on our street," said Jamie Muskrat of China Spring.
“It also brings people together because they get to hang out and talk and actually communicate, whether being on the phone or texting, "said Lyla, a China Spring resident.

articles.title_orig: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a ‘mistake’
articles.title_zh: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a ‘mistake’
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.content_orig:
Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details.
Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television.
"At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves."
Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.
Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.
The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days.
President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future.
"What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon."
Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since.
Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with.
"I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said.
Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles.
The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles' speed and trajectory.
The location of the missile site was not revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran's missile capabilities and counter past U.S. claims to have destroyed the missile program, amid fears that the war with the United States could heat up once again.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard's Aerospace Force, boasted that Iran's "capabilities have expanded significantly," adding, "We have integrated 'surprises' and highly effective assets into our combat structure."
Two tankers were attacked on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States, British maritime agency UKMTO said.
"A tanker transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz has been hit on the stern by an unknown projectile. There are no reported casualties at this time," the agency said, adding that another tanker was struck in its engine room.
Also on Saturday, Iran said it shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the strait, according to Iranian state TV.
American fighter jets struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm last Tuesday, according to a U.S. military official.
Before the Middle East war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, one fifth of the world's oil and natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has since locked down the strait and regularly targets ships that attempt to pass without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and its navy has been escorting tankers through the waterway.
Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile Friday, causing a fire onboard the vessel but no injuries, according to a British naval monitor.
The tanker was traveling out of the key waterway when it was struck by an unknown projectile, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.
The UKMTO earlier reported that a bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, had reported shots being fired in its vicinity by assailants on a small boat.
During Friday's news conference, President Trump said that during his trilateral with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping, the three leaders discussed nuclear responsibilities.
Mr. Trump said they "spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet" and that "in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship hit by drones in Baltic, Finland tightens security
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship hit by drones in Baltic, Finland tightens security
articles.content_orig:
The crew of a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland, hit by drones likely launched by Ukraine, is being evacuated into life rafts and a rescue boat.
Finnish authorities say the Sparta II has links to Russia’s armed forces and has drifted into territorial waters off Finland’s southern coast.
“There is a fire on board the ship. The situation does not pose a danger to maritime traffic or people. A restricted area has been set up around the site to ensure safety,” the Finnish Border Guard said in a statement, adding that it is in “close international cooperation” with neighbouring countries, including contact with Russia’s maritime rescue authorities.
On Saturday morning, Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with initial reports saying the ship had sustained damage. Finnish Border Guard units were dispatched to the scene, and a photograph taken by a Finnish patrol plane showed flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island, off the coast of the Finnish town of Loviisa, and Finland quickly implemented temporary air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
A Russian helicopter has since violated Finnish airspace, venturing more than 4km into Finnish territory.
“The suspected airspace violation is possibly related to rescue or tracking operations of a damaged cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. The Defence Forces and the Border Guard are handling the situation in cooperation with other authorities,” said Minister of Defence Antti Hakkanen.
By Saturday afternoon the Finnish Defence Forces said the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. Earlier, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
Finland’s Border Guard said the Sparta II is known to have links to Russia’s armed forces. The roll-on-roll-off ship was built in the year 2000 and sails under a Russian flag, according to the vesselfinder.com website.
“At the moment, ⁠⁠⁠⁠there is no confirmed information about ⁠⁠⁠⁠what cargo is on ⁠⁠⁠⁠board, but ⁠⁠⁠⁠it cannot be ruled out that there ‌‌‌‌is military materiel on board,” Iljin said.
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said damage to the ship had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
One of the major risks of attacking any vessel is environmental damage if it leaks or sinks, a scenario that Baltic Sea nations treat with high importance. That risk is “further amplified by the poor state of some of the so-called ‘Shadow Fleet’ tankers” that Russia operates, according to Robin Haggblom, senior adviser for Risk Intelligence and an expert in Finnish maritime issues.
“Actions to prevent environmental damage has also been emphasised in Finnish Border Guard communication regarding this event. Luckily in this case, we don’t yet have ice coverage in the Gulf of Finland, which would impact any oil spill recovery efforts that may be needed,” Haggblom told Al Jazeera.
The narrow and shallow waters of the Baltic Sea are some of the most crowded shipping lanes in the world. The Helsinki to Tallinn ferry route had 7.5m passenger crossings last year. Other passenger routes link Baltic ports and capital cities, and cargo vessels and military shipping contribute to the total number of vessels in the relatively small body of water.
So if Ukraine is using drones – maritime or aerial – to hit Russian ships, could there be any risks to civilian vessels?
“There obviously always is a risk of collateral damage. However, so far Ukraine does seem to be taking a number of steps to minimise the risks involved, with the Sparta II for example apparently having been identified and hit a handful of kilometres from Russian waters,” added expert Haggblom.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki later said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about strikes in the area.
“It is the same with the strike on the Russian corvette earlier, where it is reported the Ukrainians were able to pick it out and target that specific vessel among perhaps a dozen other ships. There are also unconfirmed indications that Sparta II was targeted specifically, and not just as a general Russia-associated merchant vessel,” Häggblom added.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.

articles.title_orig: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.title_zh: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.title_zh: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.title_zh: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.content_orig:
A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih , according to local authorities.
In the attack on the home city of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, ballistic missiles hit a restaurant parking lot, then jet-powered drones struck rescue workers responding, city mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said. A further drone strike hit the location for a short time later.
This latest Russian assault comes after a busy week of diplomacy, including an unprecedented meeting between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Trump described Putin as a “friend” when they met – but in a CNN interview after, Zelensky said “for us, he is a killer.”
Nearly 60 others including rescuers and police officers were injured in the initial strike and follow-up attacks, Vilkul said.
He described the events as a “tragic evening and a tragic night for our city,” adding that the attack occurred “in the city center, near a popular restaurant, on Children’s Day.” In Ukraine, Children’s Day falls on November 20 and serves as a reminder of the need to protect children’s rights and advocate for their safety.
Dramatic footage from authorities showed people moving away from debris strewn across the street, only to scramble for cover as the sound of another incoming strike rings out.
Of those wounded, 28 remain hospitalized including children , among them a three-year-old girl, as well as five people in intensive care. “Doctors are doing everything necessary to save their lives. Our condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who died… We pray for the swiftest possible recovery of the injured , ” the mayor said.
Local broadcasting outlet Rudana named the seven-year-old boy who was killed in the Russian attack as Tikhon, describing him as kind, quick-witted and talented.
The boy’s family did not live in Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelensky’s hometown, but had been in the central Ukrainian city on business and decided to stop by their favourite restaurant, the outlet reported.
“We didn’t live here because it’s dangerous… but danger caught up with us,” the boy’s mother, Olena, told the outlet. According to the report, two of Olena’s other sons are in intensive care following the strike.
Zelensky said the attack on Friday night hit an ordinary civilian area of the city. “There are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been,” he said.
“Cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions were also hit. In the Sumy region, a railway station came under attack,” the Ukrainian leader added.
Trump held talks with Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, a meeting which was followed by a large “Coalition of the Willing” gathering in Berlin, attended by European leaders as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
In a joint statement after the meeting, the group of key Ukrainian allies declared they were ready to join direct negotiations with Moscow, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Russia’s “maximalist demands are not realistic.”
Zelensky on Saturday described the three-way meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi as “very unsuccessful” for the Russian leader, who he said had failed in his goal of trying to recreate a Yalta-style conference at which Allied powers divided up the postwar world in 1945 .
“China did not let itself be drawn in. As for the United States, I don’t know what went on between them and Russia in their bilateral talks, but Ukraine was not discussed. Nothing was said publicly,” Zelensky said in audio messages shared with journalists.
“So, the plan to redraw the world’s borders didn’t work out… I think the summit was a major failure for Russia.”
CNN’s Victoria Butenko and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US historic talks: What comes next?
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US historic talks: What comes next?
articles.content_orig:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026.
The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.
The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.
The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza , where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.
A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.
“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.
Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.
Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the West
The National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.
For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.
Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press , “but now the court made it clear.”
The court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.
In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.
“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement . “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”
The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.
The court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.
It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding.
“Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.
Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.
Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia .
The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.
Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.
Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.
Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee Camp
Rohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images
But many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”
Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”
Eyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.
Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Said to Face S.E.C. Probe Into Its Accounting Practices
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Said to Face S.E.C. Probe Into Its Accounting Practices
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership .
California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.
The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.
Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.
"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.title_zh: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, French President Emmanuel Macron, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff pose for a group photo during the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
CEO of St. James's Foreign Policy Group
Europe is finally ready to step into negotiations with Russia.
Following this week's meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin , European countries are set to be represented at the negotiating table alongside Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
The continent will be represented by the E5 — Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — together with NATO and the EU representation.
Crucially, they will need to speak with one voice. This is particularly important given the recent dig directed at Europeans by President Trump's son-in-law and chief negotiator Jared Kushner during the talks in Abu Dhabi, where the European representatives were relegated to the sidelines.
The date and format of the next "quad" meeting have yet to be confirmed, but securing Europe's seat at the table is progress, particularly as Russia continues to demand a fundamental redrawing of the European security architecture.
Future negotiations will have to build on the modest achievements of the earlier talks in Saudi Arabia and subsequent diplomatic exchanges of American envoys with the Russians.
Whether Moscow has demonstrated any genuine willingness to compromise is yet to be seen.
The exact outcomes of Steve Witkoff's and Jared Kushner's visit to Moscow on Nov. 12 remain unknown, as do the details of what they have conveyed to President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. But just hearing the snippets of the meeting in the Kremlin that have almost certainly been deliberately made public makes it clear that Putin has not moved an inch away from his maximalist demands.
The set of demands made during the Istanbul negotiations in March 2022 remains unchanged: no foreign troops, the disarmament of Ukraine, neutral status and full exposure to Russian occupation with no external interference.
In November 2026, the negotiations have come full circle.
It's not surprising that Zelensky insists that Russia is not ready for peace. Moreover, as the Russian saying goes, "the appetite comes during the meal."
One can argue that Putin did not just return to his demands from the first months of the invasion; he went back to the ones he made to former U.S. President Joe Biden in 2021.
Putting the issue of "European security architecture" on the negotiating table — especially as Europeans themselves are not at said table — only proves the point Ukraine has been trying to make for almost five years of full-scale invasion: if you don't stop Putin in Ukraine, he will go for Europe.
Undoubtedly, it is Europe's strong resolve to support Ukraine, while the United States has stepped back from providing military and financial aid, that has caused an allergic reaction in the Kremlin.
Moreover, Europe's newfound determination to enhance its own defense and deterrence capabilities has sent Russia a strong signal —  and, importantly, it's time for Europe to accelerate, not stop right now.
“We are back in the world of predators.”
Many important steps have already been taken: Europe is no longer critically dependent on Russian oil and gas, nor is it willing to put business ahead of its security.
Having witnessed Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine for almost five years, and faced with uncertainty over the once unquestionably reliable transatlantic alliance, the EU has made a fundamental shift — from being primarily an economic community to one with a geopolitical agency and defense readiness as one of its key priorities.
"We are back in the world of predators," as the former long-serving Secretary-General of the European Parliament and now advisor to the EU Defense Commissioner, Klaus Welle, put it. Europe has realized that it needs to become stronger to survive in this world.
Brussels has started actively discussing the future of European security architecture with Ukraine at its center, and ways to operationalize Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union – the EU's own mutual assistance clause similar to NATO 's Article 5.
It has also boosted its defense spending in the Multiannual Financial Framework, established a dedicated Security and Defense Committee in the European Parliament , and is trying to better align national defense industries to enhance interoperability, thus translating industrial capacity into joint capability planning.
Separately, to move away from a paralyzing veto power and towards a qualified majority vote in decision-making (think Hungary), Europe is looking towards creating a brand new intergovernmental arrangement parallel to the EU, like a European Defense Union with a European Security Council as its governing body.
Ukraine is being discussed as one of its most critical members who will be shaping a new military doctrine for the European pillar of NATO.
Naturally, these gradual but unprecedented moves in the EU have ruffled some feathers in the Kremlin, prompting it to put the issue of the European security architecture up for discussion.
The Europeans, realizing that they must reestablish their agency in securing an acceptable end to the war on their continent, are now seeking broader representation in negotiations with Russia.
The fact that the EU has now taken on a greater share of financial support for Ukraine gives it a valid argument with the Americans, and $300 billion in Russian sovereign assets held in Belgium adds some leverage over Russians.
There are even talks about appointing a permanent EU envoy to Russia. A clear mandate for the position, as well as the candidacy itself, has not been drawn up yet, with many names being thrown in the ring, but the willingness to take more initiative is reassuring.
Europe should get involved in ceasefire negotiations in Ukraine, as it will be European troops observing that ceasefire.
British, French, and other European troops have been preparing for that mission, including through exercises in Poland. But even more so, Ukraine has now become an indispensable part of the European community.
This realization has finally become irreversible, not just in Kyiv but also in Brussels.
As Ukraine progresses towards its formal accession to the EU , many talks in Brussels focus on how to bring Ukraine closer sooner.
"Ukraine’s perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent’s net security provider."
There have been several attempts to float the idea of associate membership, which understandably caused a painful reaction in Ukraine, with fears of being trumped — in all the new senses of the word — but behind closed doors European officials are reassuring that this, on the contrary, is a way to bring the country at war into European structures sooner.
Others are suggesting replacing the word "associate" with "progressive" membership.
Such wordplay may seem negligible to the outsider, but within the EU corridors they can significantly shift the dynamic for an aspiring member.
Regardless, Ukraine's perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent's net security provider.
Europe has now accepted the fact that the best chance it has for strategic self-sufficiency in defense is by building on Ukraine's acquired battlefield experience and defense innovation.
Naturally, Ukrainian drone innovation takes center stage, but perhaps even more valuable is the new military doctrine taking shape in Ukraine. It is not only about cheaper, more agile hardware but the smart and sophisticated ways of deploying it — a panoply of terrain navigation, electronic warfare, the application of AI-driven C4ISR, anticipation of Russia's next move, and denial of action — ultimately, the most successful operationalization of data on the battlefield in modern history.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.
Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.
Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.
The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.
New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.
Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.
While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.
On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

articles.title_orig: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.title_zh: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.content_orig:
A survey of AI proxy services suggests stablecoins have become a key payment rail for Chinese users accessing restricted US models
Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 10:35 EST · 2 min read
Every time a major US AI lab ships a new frontier model, a shadow market on the other side of the Pacific starts paying up. In stablecoins.
That is the core finding of a new report from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. It found that payments from wallets suspected of links to China jumped 55% above baseline within three days of key US AI model releases.
Export controls were meant to keep advanced American AI out of reach. Instead, they appear to have created demand for a middleman economy, and crypto is helping settle the bill.
The report, published on November 21, 2026, describes a market where Chinese users reach restricted US frontier AI models through proxy or agent services. These services act as go-betweens, offering access that export controls would otherwise block.
Chainalysis surveyed 100 of these service providers. Of those, 40% accept payment in crypto, with stablecoins doing most of the work.
The timing pattern is what makes the data stand out. Activity from suspected China-linked wallets did not just drift upward over time. It spiked right after new US models dropped, which Chainalysis read as a sign of a coordinated rush to tap the latest capabilities.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Chainalysis described an ecosystem with increasingly specialized roles.
Access suppliers provide the underlying connection to US models. Brokers connect buyers to that access. Payment processors handle the money side of the transaction.
Some of those payment players go a step further. According to the report, certain processors obscure stablecoin transactions by routing them through third-party channels, making the trail harder to follow.
The economics help explain why. Chainalysis noted that paying for proxy access is cheaper than training comparable models from scratch. Users can query US models and distill those capabilities into local systems, essentially learning from the output rather than building the foundation themselves.
The AI findings build on earlier Chainalysis work. A report released in October 2026 had already flagged a significant rise in peer-to-peer stablecoin transactions from China-linked wallets, despite domestic restrictions on crypto trading.
That October report recorded $104.1 billion in self-custodied stablecoin transfers from China-linked wallets. Those transfers came across 18.1 million transactions between July 2025 and June 2026.
Over the past year, the Chinese crypto ecosystem has been estimated at at least $176 billion. Peer-to-peer activity accounted for 59.1% of that total.

articles.title_orig: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.title_zh: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.content_orig:
As Jensen Huang games out a possible return to Nvidia as CEO, the 63-year-old chip mogul is turning to a pocket-sized lifeline: his phone.
On the other end of the line are a series of tech CEOs, Nvidia employees, and President Donald Trump, who are offering kind words and positing avenues by which he could return to the helm .
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," venture capitalist Gavin Baker said recently in an interview on CNBC. "I think he has more to contribute to America, to AI, and technology."
Huang resigned on November 12 in the wake of accusations that he had at least two affairs, one with a Chinese executive that US intelligence says is spying for Beijing and another with a direct report at Nvidia. Huang has since indicated an interest in returning as CEO.
In a lengthy X post five days after he resigned, Huang said he's seen an "outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO."
"Many continue to reach out to me directly," he added.
Nvidia's board, however, has said that it has no plans to reinstate the founder, who wrote in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori Huang.
Here's what some influential people say they told Huang.
Trump says he called Jensen Huang at least twice since news of his affairs broke.
In a White House press conference three days before Huang resigned, Trump said he'd called Huang that day "just to see if he's feeling all right."
Trump said he asked Huang whether he knew that Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of Megaspeed and his alleged paramour, was a spy for China. Trump said Huang said he didn't know.
Then, in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, Trump said Huang called him at a separate time, telling the president that he feels bad for what he's done to his family.
The New York Times reported that in one of those calls, Trump urged Huang to fight to keep his job.
Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber who now heads an AI robotics firm called Atoms, said he wrote Huang with an auspicious promise.
"I will show up to Nvidia HQ with a wafer-encrusted megaphone, with tons of Nvidia employees who want to walk out, tons of CEOs, founders," he said recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin.
Kalanick resigned from Uber in 2017 under pressure following an investigation into its workplace culture. He said he told Huang that a petition for a CEO's return was good, but a walkout was better.
"Let's fight for what's right," Kalanick said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he's spoken with Jensen Huang since the scandal.
"It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen," Altman said at The New York Times DealBook summit.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman, sitting beside Altman, said he and his wife are friends with Huang's family. He said he reached out "just to be there for him."
Asked whether Huang thinks he can return as CEO, Altman said: "Greg and I have like a little more empathy toward the situation than the average person."
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he texted Huang to let the Nvidia founder know he is thinking of him.
"I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said at a media roundtable on November 17.
At the DealBook summit, Nadella called the situation "pretty tragic."
Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said his "most consistent message" to Huang has been to work out and maintain healthy habits.
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," Baker said on CNBC. "Because to be a sound mind, he needs to be a sound body."
Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at the hedge fund Atreides Management, said he considers Huang a friend and added that Huang has more to contribute to AI.

articles.title_orig: Honda, Toyota Recall 1.6M Vehicles Over Airbag Risk
articles.title_zh: Honda, Toyota Recall 1.6M Vehicles Over Airbag Risk
articles.content_orig:
Toyota is recalling 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles in the United States over passenger airbag inflators that could rupture, sending metal fragments toward occupants and risking serious injury or death.
Toyota is recalling more than 314,000 vehicles in the U.S. because front passenger airbag inflators made by Takata could rupture and hurl metal fragments at occupants, increasing the risk of serious injury or death.
The recall affects 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles from the 2002 through 2017 model years, according to a report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and reported by Reuters.
Affected models include the Toyota Corolla, Tundra, Sequoia and 4Runner, along with the Lexus SC430, IS250 and GX460.
FORD RECALLS 60,000 TRANSIT VANS OVER SOFTWARE GLITCH THAT SHUTS OFF LIGHTS
Certain Toyota 4Runner sport utility vehicles are included in Toyota's recall of 314,029 U.S. vehicles over Takata front passenger airbag inflators that may rupture. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Toyota reported no ruptures involving the affected inflators, according to the NHTSA recall report.
The problem stems from Takata front passenger airbag inflators that are nearing the end of their estimated safe service life. NHTSA said the inflators could rupture due to propellant degradation after long-term exposure to high humidity, high temperatures and high temperature cycling.
If the front passenger airbag deploys in a crash, the degraded inflator could rupture and send sharp metal fragments into the cabin.
POPULAR TIRE BRAND RECALLS TIRES OVER HIDDEN DEFECT THAT COULD CAUSE A SUDDEN CRASH WHILE DRIVING
Toyota Motor Corp's logo at a dealership in Tokyo, Japan, April 3, 2025. (Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters / Reuters)
Toyota said it is conducting the recall out of an abundance of caution, according to NHTSA.
Depending on the vehicle , authorized Toyota and Lexus dealers will replace the front passenger airbag inflator or the entire airbag assembly free of charge, the agency said.
Owners can check whether their vehicles are included in the recall by visiting NHTSA's recall database at nhtsa.gov/recalls and entering a 17-digit vehicle identification number or by contacting an authorized Toyota or Lexus dealership.
Toyota plans to mail owner notification letters between Dec. 28 and Jan. 11, according to the NHTSA filing, though owners do not have to wait for those letters to contact a dealer about repairs.

A representative for Toyota did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 PS5 Review Bombing Out of Control as Zelda Receives Revenge Ratings
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 PS5 Review Bombing Out of Control as Zelda Receives Revenge Ratings
articles.content_orig:
Update [ Sat 21st Nov 2026, 3:30pm ]:
In response to a coordinated review bombing effort on GTA 6 , fans of the Rockstar release appear to have launched a counter-attack on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , believing Nintendo gamers are to blame for the situation.
Last night, I reported that GTA 6’s Metacritic user score was racking up ‘0’ review scores at an unprecedented pace. Many of the ratings were bogus.
In the hours since, the Switch 2’s universally adored remake of Ocarina of Time has seen its user score drop from 9.6 to 8.9 at the time of writing.
One ‘0’ rating simply reads: “Take your own medicine.”
At this point, I just wish Metacritic would do away with user scores, although I’ve no doubt this sorry situation is all good for business.
The thing is: this isn’t the first time the critic aggregator has become a battleground like this. As I mentioned in my original report, many of the greatest games ever made have pitiful user scores on the site.
Hopefully this all blows over, because it’s all rather embarrassing right now.
Original Story: GTA 6 , the highest-rated game of all-time , is getting review bombed on Metacritic as idiots attempt to plunge the seminal Rockstar release’s rating with bogus ‘0’ scores.
At the time of writing, the title has a user score of 5.4 , meaning it’s considered ‘Mixed or Average’:
This is in sharp contrast to critics, who awarded the game an average score of 99, making it the best-reviewed title of all time.
“Good thing Rockstar doesn’t blacklist user ratings like they do critics,” one review reads.
There’s a theory among some online that the dev blacklists media outlets for giving its games poor scores, but it put GTA 6 in the hands of more than 150 critics, so I don’t buy that for a single second.
Many of the ‘0’ reviews all touch on the same thing: 30fps is “unplayable”, the series has gone “woke”, and the “story is horrible”. (“I never smiled one time,” writes one seemingly perpetually miserable user.)
There are some legitimate criticisms among these; one person writes they’re not a fan of the life sim elements and prefer the “power fantasy” of older games. That’s fair, but it doesn’t make it a ‘0’.
Metacritic reviews have always been a disaster really, because you don’t need to actually own a game to rate it. Many of the best titles ever released have dreadful user scores on the site.
On the PS Store , though – where you actually have to spend money on the game to score it – the current rating sits at 4.84 based on 170k reviews. So that’s probably a better reflection of how the community feels.
My take on all this is that humans are predictable creatures: wherever there’s something popular, you’re probably going to find a group of people eager to tear it down.

articles.title_orig: Modders Are Trying to Create a PC Native Version of GTA 6 With Its Leaked Xbox Series X Build
articles.title_zh: Modders Are Trying to Create a PC Native Version of GTA 6 With Its Leaked Xbox Series X Build
articles.content_orig:
Just when it seemed Cyberleek had disappeared for good, the notorious leaker has returned. Even though the GTA 6 release date has passed, the individual has followed through on past threats. A decrypted Xbox build is spreading through piracy networks, which could lead to a playable PC port . However, there is one major caveat with the 209 GB download.
The Cyberleek website now displays a message about the latest leak. While prior gameplay videos appeared to be from a PC-based development build , they elected to distribute GTA 6 Xbox files. Allegedly, this version is from November 2026, and images of a file structure exposing assets have emerged. Regardless, it may have limited use without the missing executable file.
Once again, Cyberleek hopes to raise cryptocurrency funds before releasing the critical file. Offering a playable build as the reward, they previously set a $30 million market capitalization goal for a meme coin. That October initiative failed, but hitting the $15 million mark will supposedly unlock the .exe.
Notably, a timer is also counting down from under 4 days. Once it expires, Rockstar ’s tormentor promises to circulate the executable on piracy sites anyway.
It's unclear how soon the GTA 6 Xbox files may result in a bootable game for PC users. Cyberleek believes hackers will find a way to emulate the console version for Windows within a week. As criticism of the 30 fps performance target continues, capable hardware could produce higher frame rates.
Unfortunately for pirates, no working Series X emulator currently exists. The hardware found in the Microsoft console and many PCs is similar, with CPUs sharing x86-64 architecture. Still, among other challenges, the Series X runs a custom OS that would need to be adapted for a Windows environment.
Another possibility is a decompilation project targeting the leaked GTA 6 Xbox files. Developers would analyze, modify, and reconstruct the code into a version that can boot on PCs.
Cyberleek also claims to possess a PS5 build as a fallback option. Besides accumulating cryptocurrency, the objective is to prevent console and PC ports from doubling Take-Two and Rockstar's profits.

articles.title_orig: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.title_zh: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.content_orig:
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.
