articles.title_orig: The Fastest Way To Increase Focus Levels In ‘GTA 6’
articles.title_zh: The Fastest Way To Increase Focus Levels In ‘GTA 6’
articles.content_orig:
First introduced back in GTA 5 alongside Red Dead's Deadeye system, Focus Mode is back for both Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI , with a few cool upgrades. This official IGN GTA 6 guide teaches you how Focus works, including while in and out of combat, when pinpointing the source of a noise, and when tracking vehicles and animals.
Click on a link below to jump to that specific section of this guide:
Unlike in GTA 5 where Franklin, Michael, and Trevor each had their own unique special abilities, Focus Mode works the same way for both main characters in GTA 6 and feels a lot like Michael's classic bullet-time ability.
You can trigger Focus Mode by clicking in both sticks ( Left Stick Click + Right Stick Click / Left Stick Click + Right Stick Click ) the same time , though how it works changes slightly depending on whether you’re actively in combat or not.
Enabling Focus slows down time and highlights interactive objects around you. If you aren't actively aiming down sights or shooting, Focus Mode won't drain your meter at all – even when you're behind the wheel.
When you aren't aiming, Focus Mode helps you spot openable doors, color-coded loot, and bad guys. It lasts for 30 seconds when on foot and has a two-second cooldown once the 30-second limit has been exhausted. That said, you can reactivate it immediately if you haven’t drained the full 30 seconds.
When you use Focus while driving, you get extra breathing room to pull off tricky driving maneuvers. It won't boost your vehicle's handling like Franklin's ability used to in GTA 5, but the extra reaction time makes a huge difference when you're dodging cops or rival gangs. Plus, police officers glow blue, making them easy to spot and avoid in areas where you are wanted.
Focus Mode lasts for 30 seconds when driving, though this is affected by speed: the faster you go, the less time you get in Focus Mode. It can drop to as low as 10 seconds if you’re driving super fast. It also has a two-second cooldown between uses. Everything interactive is color-coded while Focus Mode is active:
You'll also see weapons lying on the ground highlighted in red, so you can grab them easily.
Your meter drains if you aim when using Focus in combat - this is called Combat Focus . When you line up a shot on an enemy, you'll see yellow and red target spots appear on their body as the meter depletes.
Yellow spots indicate limbs where shots will wound or disarm them – aiming for a hand can make them drop their gun, while hitting a leg can knock them down. Red spots mark lethal target areas on the head and heart for quick kills. Target hotspots aren't just for enemies; they show up on vehicles too. For land vehicles, aim for the tires or engine block to quickly disable them. If you're dealing with helicopters, target the engine or rotor assemblies to bring them down.
Keep in mind that aiming in Combat Focus burns through your meter fast. A quick way to refill your meter when you're out of combat is to smoke a cigarette. Additionally, if Jason/Lucia’s Criminal Profile is Professional, incapacitations boosts your meter. If their Criminal Profile is Violent or worse, landing headshots increases it instead.
Another main use for Focus Mode while out in the world is to use it to find noises. Often, an event can be happening close by, but you may not be able to tell exactly where it is coming from. Focus Mode will show sound ripples in the air, pointing you directly to the action. This is incredibly useful for scoping out Side Missions and activities, as it will help tell the difference between an NPC just talking to someone else or the start of an activity or Side Mission. These ripples will also appear for any police cars, K9 dogs, and helicopters that are actively searching for you while you’re Wanted, plus any witnesses to the crime.
Tracking returns in GTA 6, and Focus is the way to do it! When chasing down a vehicle during a mission, using Focus will show their trails, allowing you to keep up with where they are heading. Similarly, the animal tracking mechanic returns from Red Dead Redemption 2. When hunting for wildlife, entering Focus Mode will show you scent trails for various creatures, going so far as to inform you what animal is making the scent.
Luckily, you don’t need to stay locked into Focus when tracking wildlife, as there’s a prompt to track a specific animal and it will stay on your screen even after exiting Focus Mode.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6’s $80 price hides a surprise for American families
articles.title_zh: GTA 6’s $80 price hides a surprise for American families
articles.content_orig:
While base prices have remained steady or lower over time, the video game industry is relying more on microtransactions.
After 13 years, the latest installment of Grand Theft Auto is finally coming out on Thursday and will set players back $80 for the standard version and $100 if you opt for the Ultimate Edition with bonus features. While the price tag is higher than the standard $60 or $70 many gamers have gotten used to, the franchise has actually gotten cheaper after you adjust for inflation.
GTA: San Andreas sold for $50 back in 2004 (or $89 in today's dollars), while IV cost $60 when it was released in 2008 ($94 in today's dollars) and V also cost $60 for the standard edition when it was sold in 2013 (roughly $87 after adjusting for inflation).
GTA VI's parent company spent $1 billion to $1.5 billion to make the game, according to estimates.
The transition from physical media to digital, the expansion of the global market and the rise of microtransactions have helped keep prices across the gaming industry stable, experts told Marketplace. But while prices have actually gone down over time, some players have expressed concern about how microtransactions have eroded the gaming experience and what GTA VI's base prices will mean for industry prices going forward.
The cost of producing physical media, including the actual disc and the packaging, is "not trivial," said Andrew Ching, a marketing professor at Johns Hopkins University.
The transition to digital lowered those costs, and also reduced middlemen costs since customers could bypass third-party retailers and purchase a game directly through their console, Ching explained.
While research and development costs have risen over time, the global market for video games was able to expand quickly, leading to an increased volume in sales, Ching said.
The video game industry also began relying more on online subscription services and microtransactions, requiring users to pay for additional in-game features. Rockstar sells a GTA+ membership for $7.99 a month for GTA Online users. GTA Online alone rakes in an estimated $500 million a year for Rockstar.
"Buying the base game is kind of like your entry point into a kind of ecosystem which can extract further revenue, so there's a dark side," said Michael Hamilton, an assistant professor of operations management at Baruch College in New York.
So while consumers have seen video game prices remain steady, revenues haven't stagnated, Hamilton said.
"They have moved the monetization away from that initial purchase and into these small transactions, and I think — a lot of times — in a way that makes the product a worse experience," Hamilton said.
Some gamers are worried that GTA's $80 and $100 price tags will lead to rising prices across the industry (the game's release follows Nintendo Switch 2’s Mario Kart World, which also had an $80 price tag).
However, GTA VI might be an unusual case given that it's expected to be the biggest video game release of all time. It's predicted to rake in $3 billion to $5 billion in sales in its first week and cause millions of employees to call in sick.
The industry might use the GTA's price to test the waters and raise prices for other games, but Ching said he thinks it could be harder for others to match that price and be successful.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.content_orig:
PC gamers' enormous thirst for Grand Theft Auto VI is leading them to go to extraordinary lengths to play Rockstar 's latest masterpiece on their PC with additional features.
A few days ago, we reported that a tool called SmoovPlay claimed to be able to stream the game on PC at up to 120 frames per second with optional frame generation and upscaling. Now, a similar tool called Veyra also promises NVIDIA DLSS 5 injection to further augment the game's already excellent visuals.
Veyra, or Veyra-NRVideo to give it its full name, pitches itself bluntly on GitHub : " Bring PS5 GTA6 to 120FPS with DLSS 5 ." It's a free GPL-3.0 Windows 11 application that applies GPU enhancement to a video source in real time, and it has clearly gotten the community excited, racking up 4.9k stars and 333 forks, with version 2.2.0 released just yesterday. The source can be a capture card, a PS5 over Remote Play, a PC stream via Sunshine, an Xbox (which the project labels unofficial and experimental), or simply a window on your desktop.
Everything is rendered through DirectX 12, and the project ships separate NVIDIA and AMD builds. What it layers on top is the upscaler stack (NVIDIA DLSS, Intel XeSS, and AMD FSR as selectable super-resolution options), NVIDIA DLAA, neural denoising, HDR handling, and frame generation, arranged either as an ordered effects list or a node-based chain. You can check out a video showing off Grand Theft Auto VI run through Veyra below.
Veyra isn't the only route. NeuralScreen takes a broader approach, applying DLSS 5 neural rendering to the entire Windows desktop in real time with support claimed for NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 30, 40, and 50 Series cards.
GameGPU ran GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro , captured through an AVerMedia Live Gamer ULTRA 2.1 GC553G2 into a system with an RTX 5090 and a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and applied NVIDIA DLSS 5's Natural profile alongside 6X frame generation via NeuralScreen v2.6.4. The result at 4K was a stable 262 to 280 FPS , with peaks of 286 FPS, with the 5090 sitting at 62-75% utilization, drawing 305-368W, and using around 5.3 GB of video memory.
Of course, none of this actually makes Grand Theft Auto VI run faster . The game is still rendering at 30 FPS on the console; everything downstream is interpolation and post-processing applied to a video signal. The 280 FPS counter indicates improved motion smoothness on the display, but certainly not better responsiveness, which feels worse due to increased input latency compared to playing directly on the console .
A capture card should fare better than PS5's Remote Play here, since it carries the HDMI signal directly rather than encoding, transmitting, and decoding it across a network. However, it's still just a workaround whose benefits may very well be outweighed by the negatives . The only real appeal is the DLSS 5 injection, but even that cannot compare to the proper injection we see regularly in PC games. That is because DLSS 5 needs color and motion vectors to perform at its best; in this case, it cannot have either, so it's applied to Grand Theft Auto VI much like it would be to any video.
If the latest rumors are correct, though, we may not have to wait long for the real PC version , with GamesBeat sources suggesting Rockstar might target a Q1 2027 launch .
About the author : With over two decades of experience in gaming journalism, Alessio Palumbo has led the gaming vertical at Wccftech since August 2015. He started working at a young age for Italian websites like Everyeye.it, Gamestar.it, Nextgame.it, and Multiplayer.it before kickstarting the indie English-language publication Worlds Factory as its founder and Editor in Chief. 

In the last decade, he has coordinated the overall output of Wccftech's gaming section, managed PR relations, assigned reviews, produced daily news coverage, edited gaming content as needed, and delivered game reviews.  

Arguably, his trademark content is the long series of exclusive developer interviews that have been cited by Wikipedia and by the biggest news media and gaming publications. 

His passion for technology also makes him knowledgeable when it comes to gaming hardware and tech. His favorite genres include RPGs, MMORPGs, and action/adventure games.

articles.title_orig: PS5 Survives GTA 6's Unfathomably Humongous Launch without a Hitch
articles.title_zh: PS5 Survives GTA 6's Unfathomably Humongous Launch without a Hitch
articles.content_orig:
We’d rightly criticise Sony if the PS5 had fallen to pieces during GTA 6’s launch, so let’s give the platform holder a nod of approval for navigating these past two weeks almost flawlessly.
There were some minor scattered instances of PSN outages on Wednesday evening prior to the Rockstar title’s big launch, but these never affected everyone and the network recovered pretty fast. I think we can give that a pass.
Meanwhile, the preload process worked flawlessly as far as I’m aware. I haven’t really seen any widespread reporting of people being unable to download the game in advance of its release.
Given its size and the sheer number of people wanting to play – remember, 32.5 million copies were sold across all consoles prior to release – that’s a humongous strain on Sony’s servers, which is predicted to have accounted for approximately 75% of all purchases.
Obviously GTA 6 is a single player-only game , so that certainly put less stress on the PSN as a whole, and the new GTA Online’s eventual launch will be an even bigger test – but for now, the PS5 has held up remarkably well.
I’m not saying we should get out the champagne – this is the experience consumers quite rightly expect Sony to deliver.
But this was still a huge, unprecedented test for PlayStation’s infrastructure – and it’s fair to say it navigated it almost flawlessly. In my opinion, that deserves acknowledging at least.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year . Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom.
Snider’s note said the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days.
Goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged.
Goldman said any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning.
Condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40 times trailing sales for Anthropic. A US Bank Asset Management executive said the valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” Goldman’s own outlook says the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond “is highly uncertain.”
Condition 2: the Fed. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, and the Fed meets Dec. 9. Goldman’s economists expect hikes in December and March, sending the federal funds rate to a peak of 4.25% to 4.5%. A dovish signal looks unlikely soon. Treasuries did rally sharply Friday as investors looked for safety, which is not the same as a Fed pivot. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%.
Condition 3: A big drop in investor positioning. This has often marked the end of past drawdowns.
The first condition is unsettled, to say the least. Anthropic’s historic IPO turned into a sort of referendum on the entire AI trade, an unfair weight to put on a single, albeit remarkably important, company. The company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, passing SpaceX’s $85.7 billion as the biggest IPO on record. The shares jumped 17% on Thursday, then gave most of it back Friday to close at $88.91 , not far above the $83 IPO price. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly,” said Dakota Wealth’s Robert Pavlik. “I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company… I think they’re just skeptical of this market.” Morgan Stanley , the underwriter tasked with stabilizing the shares, closed its support position , removing a potential pillar of support.
UBS said the debate had shifted from whether AI investment will continue to whether it can generate enough revenue and returns for shareholders. A Capital Economics economist wrote that the IPO’s success while other AI stocks fell shows the parts of the AI ecosystem “no longer move as one,” as chipmakers Nvidia , Broadcom , Micron and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14% .
Nvidia’s 14% fall on Friday was its worst day in almost two years. It lost 22.9% on the week and is down 47.5% since Oct. 6, a loss of $2.7 trillion in market value. Reuters reported the SEC is probing its accounting practices . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 , and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The VIX, Wall Street’s “Fear Gauge,” closed at 35.89, its highest in 19 months .
“It’s a meltdown right now,” said Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research. JPMorgan Asset Management’s David Kelly took the other view: “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu.”
On the third condition, Goldman’s note says hedge funds have already cut back. Their net leverage is the lowest since April 2025. A companion report, Snider’s Hedge Fund Trend Monitor, says the most popular hedge fund longs were crowded into the AI trade and have lagged the S&P 500 by 14 percentage points over six months. That is among the worst stretches in the basket’s 20-year history. The note described the situation for hedge funds as “bruised and broadening.”
But Goldman’s broader Sentiment Indicator is still above average. U.S. equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in nearly $170 billion in the fourth quarter so far. Asset managers’ net equity futures positions are in the 82nd percentile of the past 10 years. Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. Goldman Research says AI capital spending produced “about half” of this year’s earnings growth.
The Street is split on whether this is the top. Capital Economics expects further declines. Goldman’s Nov. 17 outlook , written before the drop, forecast 8,700 by the end of 2027. In the Nov. 20 note, its range runs from about 5,800 to 8,100 depending on whether investors regain confidence in earnings. From Friday’s close, that is roughly 16% downside and 17% upside. Those percentages are my math, not Goldman’s.
After the 22 S&P 500 corrections since 1980, the index averaged a 4% return over the next three months. It rose in 17 of them. E*Trade’s research is less reassuring. Of the 14 times since 1983, the index first closed 10% or more below a record, five became bear markets.
Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune 's executive editor of global news.

articles.title_orig: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble
articles.title_zh: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble
articles.content_orig:
Don’t panic about the AI bubble, folks — just ignore all the economists hyperventilating about it in the corner.
The absurdly swift rise of Anthropic has experts feeling baffled and gloomy about the future of Wall Street. Becoming a $1.5 trillion dollar company, after its blockbuster IPO finalized Wednesday, in just a matter of years is unprecedented, signaling that AI is sending our economy into yet more unprecedented territory. And that uncertainty is scary.
“No company in history has grown so big, so fast,” David B. Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor, told the Washington Post .
And the pressure is on, he added: “Expectations for continued rapid growth will be off the charts.”
Talk of a bubble has loomed over the industry for years, but investors have been antsier of late. More than ever, they fear that the trillions being poured into AI won’t lead to a return on investment in the near future. Google’s market cap plummeted by half a trillion dollars in a day last month, WaPo noted, after its earnings showed that its chief source of revenue, search advertising, was growing more slowly than predicted because of its difficulty monetizing its AI search features that are also pushing users away from seeing traditional search ads.
The most promising avenue for AI making money was through enterprise sales. Corporate customers and businesses were happily paying for access to frontier coding tools from major labs like Anthropic. But many customers have since been rattled by the often exorbitant costs of using these AI tools — one immortal example: a company that reportedly blew $500 million on Claude tokens in a single month — and have placed tighter spending limits or adopted a hybrid approach of using a mix of cheaper Chinese models as an alternative.
There’s also been the sort of fantasy-land salesmanship characteristic of the hubris an industry exudes before the bubble inevitably bursts. This summer, SpaceX rebranded itself as not just an aerospace company but also an AI one before going public, with CEO Elon Musk promising investors that it would start generating $1 trillion in annual revenue before the end of the decade. Even more incredibly, the company predicted it would potentially make $26.5 trillion in AI sales down the line — more than the GDP of the entire nation of China.
“It’s already a bubble,” Gary Gensler, an MIT economist and the former head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, told CNN this week.
Gensler pointed to the mountains of cash being poured into AI infrastructure, which some estimates put as high as $800 billion a year.
“History tells us that when you have a new technology and a significant investment… you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” said Gensler. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.”
The performance of Anthropic’s newly minted stock, which investors hoped would deliver tech stocks out of a weekslong rally , is no less concerning. Insider investors immediately cashed in on the initial rally and sent its stock into free-fall, tumbling by 12 percent today. It echoed into other tech stocks, sending the Nasdaq down by 3.7 percent.
“I can’t say exactly when and how stormy,” Gensler said of the looming threat of a bursting bubble, “but I would be battening down some hatches and making sure you have some proper rain gear.”

articles.title_orig: Tentative Deal Averts Strike Threat at Busiest U.S. Ports
articles.title_zh: Tentative Deal Averts Strike Threat at Busiest U.S. Ports
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Workers at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could go on strike as soon as Saturday as the expiration of their contract looms.
A strike would disrupt cargo movement during a key holiday shipping period and amid the busiest year on record for the two ports combined.
ILWU Local 26, a union that represents about 250 security guards at the ports, has been in negotiations with port employers for more than a year after its contract first expired in July 2025.
Union members in Wilmington marched in solidarity and celebration Monday, but worry about future jobs and the cost of living, all as politicians court their votes.
Although Local 26 includes only about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the ports, thousands of longshoremen and marine clerks are expected to honor the picket line and cease working if there is a strike.
Members of Local 26 work at port terminals that handle roughly 85% of cargo at the Port of Long Beach and 33% at the Port of Los Angeles. The union has already voted to authorize a strike.
“The union has indicated an unwillingness to extend the contract beyond its expiration at 12:01 a.m. on Saturday, November 21, setting up the real potential for a strike at the nation’s busiest port complex,” said the Pacific Maritime Assn., which represents employers at the port.
Local 26’s demands have not materially changed since negotiations began, the assn. said.
The Port of Los Angeles announced it moved more cargo in September than in any other single month in its history.
Members of Local 26, known as watchmen, perform security duties including credential checks and routine patrols at six container terminals.
The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Pacific Maritime Assn. has offered a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each Local 26 member and has made a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000.
The offer also maintains healthcare benefits for active workers and retirees and increases pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure.
The Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach are considering a joint incentive program that would provide $60 in funding for electric cargo trucks per one-way trip.
The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service has stepped in to guide negotiations, but has not made progress.
“The impact would reach tens of thousands of workers locally and hundreds of thousands more across the national intermodal network,” the Pacific Maritime Assn said. “ Truck drivers would sit idle, rail shipments would be disrupted, and warehouse workers could see their hours cut.”

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title_orig: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.title_zh: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.content_orig:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020
articles.title_zh: Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020
articles.content_orig:
Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar.
"This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company.
Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.
It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge , which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020.
Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence.
That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple , Microsoft , Alphabet , Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX .
With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits.
After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025.
Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar.
"There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP.  The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said.
Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus.
For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said.
Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to."
"At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that."
Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation."
That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic missed its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money."
Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to use alternatives from Amazon and Google as well. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier.
"It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics showed it was "going to be a very high-quality business."
Anthropic isn't the only big win for VCs this year.
Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz.
SpaceX and Anthropic alone will make 2026 a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other year in IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering.
IVP's Dash said that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027.
The macro picture, however, is ominous.
Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the company already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board.
In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would push Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range.
Narasin said he wasn't even sure the company would get that far.
"I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin said.
That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering.
"This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin said. "There was a company that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.title_zh: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here .
Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks , United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.
So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs . Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.
Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates . Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”
External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.
“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”
IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.
“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”
Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.
Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000 . To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.
In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.
There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”
Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher , at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.
“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”
Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.
• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters . The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.
• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “ wrench attacks ”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage .
• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports , the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.
That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas.
Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.
"In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .
He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.)
Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.)
The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.
Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions , and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.
So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.
"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.
And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.
This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites , and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that .
Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title_orig: My Mother-in-Law Only Wants to Talk About One Creepy Thing at Family Gatherings. I Can’t Take Another Minute.
articles.title_zh: My Mother-in-Law Only Wants to Talk About One Creepy Thing at Family Gatherings. I Can’t Take Another Minute.
articles.content_orig:
Azhar Al-Ruabie is a freelance journalist in Iraq
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.
The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.
His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.
“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph , his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”
The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.
When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.
He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.
“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.
To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.
HIV is generally stigmatised in Iraq and across the Middle East. Mehdi finds it difficult to talk about his illness with friends or even doctors. So he began talking to ChatGPT and asking it about his treatment and how his life with HIV is likely to pan out.
Dr Riyadh Abdulameer Al-Hilfi, head of the general health directorate at Iraq’s Ministry of Health, agreed that HIV-related stigma is the main challenge for many people with the virus. “No one is prepared for people to know that they have HIV – it is difficult,” he said.
Dr Al-Hilfi added: “Some prominent Iraqis known to be HIV-positive seek treatment abroad to avoid being judged or discovered by society.”
In 2025, 902 people tested positive for HIV across Iraq, mostly young men, but the infection remains far below epidemic levels, says Al-Hilfi .
According to the UNAIDS 41 million people were living with HIV worldwide in 2025. That year, 1.2 million people newly acquired HIV, and half a million people died from Aids-related illnesses.
In the Middle East/North Africa region, UNAIDS estimates that 240,000 people were living with HIV in 2025, alongside 22,000 new HIV infections and 6,600 Aids-related deaths.
The HIV/Aids control programme was adopted by the Iraqi Ministry of Health in 1987 in response to the first case detected in the country, when blood for haemophiliacs was found to be carrying the virus. The virus is believed to have entered Iraq through imported products supplied by a French company.
“That year between 4,000 to 4,700 people were diagnosed with HIV; some patients have died, but many are under treatment and in good health,” Dr Al-Hilfi added.
In recent years, the majority of people with HIV have been detected through routine blood screening. “Patients rarely cite sexual practices as the cause, and around 40 per cent say they do not know how they were infected.”
Dr Al-Hilfi stressed that anyone who adheres to the medication can live a healthy life, and that effective treatment means that HIV/Aids has become a manageable chronic disease.
However, patients complain that the HIV drug currently available can lead to side effects. It is a three-drug combination therapy manufactured in Iran which Mehdi says has led to nausea, headaches and weight loss. Other HIV patients have taken to social media to describe additional side effects from the Iranian-made drug.
“My body weight was 73kg, today I am 65kg,” Mehdi said. “But it is free of charge in state-run hospitals, so I had no option but to take it, rather than paying privately,” he said.
Instead of his daily pill he wishes he could access the long-acting injectable treatments available in Western countries.
Many Iraqis with suspected HIV avoid government health centres for testing as they worry they will share their information with security agencies, so testing numbers under-represent cases. The Telegraph spoke with patients who said it was only the free treatment that compelled them to attend.
But Dr Al-Hilfi insists that confidentiality is paramount. “Personal details are shared only with doctors, nurses and pharmacists. Security agencies once requested the names of HIV-positive patients, but we [the ministry of health] refused to share them,” he said.
In a Facebook group called “HIV in Iraq,” which has 1,700 members, Iraqis share information, their experience of living with HIV, and the challenges they face. Many share their struggles with getting hold of medication.
Mehdi and others complain that during official holidays they are unable to obtain their medication, or that doctors don’t supply the full course.
“Denying a patient the full course would be ‘abuse’ in the doctor-patient relationship,” said Dr Al-Hilfi.
The discrimination, bullying and stigma that HIV/Aids patients face has led Dr Fadhil Hussein Al-Shibly, a retired infectious diseases specialist with many years experience treating HIV, to tell his patients they are not criminals.
However, some doctors do not follow his lead.
“Ignorance unfortunately exists among doctors,” Dr Al-Shibly added. He has known surgeons refuse to operate on HIV positive patients for fear of contracting the virus.
Al-Shibly likens this to a firefighter refusing to attend a blaze because they are afraid of fire.
In the HIV center at Al-Karamah Teaching Hospital in Baghdad, Dr Maha Abdulkareem, sees about 20 to 30 patients a day. On the day The Telegraph visited the hospital five of these patients were new.
“Before I worked here I didn’t realise there were many people in Iraq living with HIV,” she said.
Dr Abdulkareem added: “I provide psychological support and do not frighten the patient about HIV. I tell them it is a chronic disease that remains for life, and we treat it as if we are treating diabetes.”
Mehdi, speaking as he sat in a café smoking shisha, agrees: “The one thing I would urge people to hold onto is this: HIV is not a death sentence. You can live with it healthily and normally, and I’m proof of that.”

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
Paul Smith, chief commercial officer of Anthropic, center left, and Krishna Rao, chief financial officer of Anthropic, center right, alongside others react during the closing bell ceremony for the Anthropic IPO at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.
