articles.title_orig: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
articles.title_zh: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
articles.content_orig:
EU thought to have backing of 130 countries in last-ditch push to get fossil fuels mentioned in outcome of UN climate summit.
After all the running down corridors, here is where we are:
After marching into the offices of the joint presidencies en masse and with “the whole world” as one participant put it, at about 6.10pm this evening in Turkey , the EU stayed in the meeting with the joint presidencies only briefly, leaving at about 6.30pm, while many developing countries and the UK stayed in.
The UK and the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) countries remained in the meeting with the presidencies for nearly an hour.
The Guardian understands that the EU left because it needed to have a coordination meeting with its member states and the high ambition coalition, to discuss its way forward.
The issue for the EU is the text under consideration. One possible version would include a reference to the UAE consensus decision at Cop28, paragraph 28 of which contained the key resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels”. This oblique reference to the phaseout of fossil fuels was also the formulation used last year at Belem.
The Guardian understands that such an oblique reference would be acceptable to the High Ambition Coalition, which comprises many developing countries, the UK and some other allies, but there is still a question mark over whether the EU member states will agree to it, or demand something stronger and more explicit.
The EU is now consulting on that.
The Guardian also understands that Saudi Arabia refused to drop its demand for carbon capture and storage (CCS) to be strongly recommended in the text, on a par with the target for electrification, and still refuses to allow any reference to the “transition away from fossil fuels”.
If this standoff continues and if Saudi continues to hold out on CCS and to refuse any references to fossil fuels, the next step – which the Guardian understands is being actively considered by the EU – could be to force a plenary, at which Saudi Arabia would have to either go along with the consensus or publicly oppose the revised wording.
This is a risky strategy, as Saudi Arabia and its allies could hold out. But Bill Hare, chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, and a longtime observer of Cops, told the Guardian it might be the only strategy left. Some believe the Arab Group is no longer as united behind Saudi Arabia as that country had assumed at the outset of these talks.
“If the overwhelming number of countries here want a strong text, referencing the transition away from fossil fuels and so on, and Saudi Arabia is on its own, I think Saudi Arabia will probably not stand against the global consensus,” Hare said.
The three key demands of the countries calling themselves the progressive coalition are now: a reference to the transition away from fossil fuels, or to the UAE Consensus decision in which that resolution appeared; for stronger wording on the tripling of adaptation finance for developing countries; and for any reference to CCS to be either removed or to be weakened and “balanced” by strong language on electrification.
The Guardian also understands that China and India, though not allied with the EU, the UK and the High Ambition Coalition and their allies, who number about 130 countries, are unlikely to stand against those countries.
A predicament “that never should have deteriorated so far” is how Jasper Inventor, head of the Greenpeace’s delegation, has described the current situation at Cop31 , as weary delegates bemoan the lack of a new draft deal or clarity over the next steps.
“The fact that no text has been distributed and no actual negotiations between parties has been happening throughout the day is a predicament, and the situation should never have deteriorated so far,” he said. “Parties need to be sitting across the table, looking each other in the eye and negotiating the text themselves, not waiting behind closed doors for the Presidency to produce a compromise.”
He added: “The climate crisis is accelerating beyond the negotiating rooms here in Antalya and yet we are still waiting for a text that aims to address the root cause of the crisis – ending fossil fuels.”
What if too many people go home? Giuliana Viglione, associate editor at Carbon Brief, has explored the prospect of Cop31 being suspended if too many delegates leave to catch flights back to their countries.
double quotation mark If and when delegations start departing the country, the Cop may be in danger of losing quorum.
According to the UNFCCC’s draft rules of procedure, two-thirds of parties must be present in order for decisions to be made. (The US is technically still a party to the convention, so this means 132 out of 198 parties to the UNFCCC – and 130 out of 194 parties to the Paris Agreement.)
A loss of quorum would mean a suspension of the talks, which would have to be resumed at a later date.
While we wait for more from the presidencies, here is an interesting sidelight on this year’s Cop. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, has been one of the stars of Antalya. His blistering attack on the state of negotiations on Wednesday became a rallying call for “climate-progressive” countries and groups.
The world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”, he told a press conference for the Fossil Fuel Anti-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. “We are in love with our kidnappers. We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”
But in another set of vital climate-related negotiations, Panama has been playing a markedly different role.
At the International Maritime Organisation, countries are working on a potential levy on the carbon dioxide emitted from international shipping. This levy has been more than a decade in development, as shipping companies and countries reliant on maritime transport have been reluctant for many years to address the 2-3% of global emissions contributed by the industry.
Two years ago, it looked as if green voices had finally won out – IMO members had agreed a framework for cutting their emissions, and a levy on carbon dioxide emissions to help it along. Money raised by the levy – which could amount to tens of billions of dollars a year – could go to help clean up shipping, but some could be diverted to help the most vulnerable countries recover from the impacts of climate catastrophe.
Then came Donald Trump. The US president was bitterly opposed, and members of his administration started a campaign to halt the levy. Some IMO participants described being bullied by the US, while others were threatened with US visa revocation if they did not back down and change their positions.
The campaign worked: at a meeting of the IMO, enough members switched their position to allow for a postponement of the levy.
Next week, at crunch meetings at the IMO headquarters in London, the talks will resume, with a further delay possible. And this time, Panama is on the side of the delayers.
Tristan Smith, professor of energy and transport at University College London, told the Guardian: “Panama’s position moved from supporting the progressive solutions – the levy and the net zero framework [to cut shipping emissions] – in the first half of 2025, to leading the discussion on the weakest alternative to the net zero framework in the first half of 2026.”
Analysis by Smith showed that Panama’s proposals would have produced higher greenhouse gas emissions than alternative plans on the table. Another group of shipping experts told the Guardian they believed there was a “major disconnect” between Panama’s environment ministry and its Maritime and Canal Authority.
As a result, the good work done for the climate at Cop could be undone at the IMO negotiations next week, if shipping interests win out over those who want to cut shipping’s emissions and use a carbon levy to help poor countries stricken by

articles.title_orig: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.title_zh: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.content_orig:
The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.
U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.
Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites , bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.
It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.
The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.
A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.
"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.
The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.
"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."
There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.
A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.
American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.
Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)
Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.
American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.
"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."
Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.
On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.
First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.
And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.
"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."
Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites , respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.
American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.
Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.
Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.
United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options , which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.
There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.
"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."
Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.
Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.
British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.
Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways , Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats .
"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

articles.title_orig: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player spins out in the open
articles.title_zh: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player spins out in the open
articles.content_orig:
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Your newsletter sign-up was successful
Want to add more newsletters?
Teenage Engineering has finally revealed its newest piece of audio gear after a month of hints and leaks. The new EP/BC–1 is the Swedish company’s first CD player – ‘a modern take on a classic CD player’ – and marks the start of a new line of equipment, the ‘broadcast series.’
This slender rectangle leaves the CD exposed atop the mechanism, with a line of red LEDs showing the precise timecode and track detail, along with output volume and – unusually – a varispeed setting that allows professionals to slow up or speed down the CD by 50% to 150%.
Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1 atop the EP-35 amplifier
The new player is designed to pair beautifully with the recently released EP-35 portable speaker and amplifier – it slots on top, held in place by the EP-35’s clips – and therefore matches the dimensions of the K.O.II groove machines .
The EP/BC-1 not only functions as a straightforward CD player, it also has digital audio output over USB 2.0, can rip audio CDs to digital files, streams via Bluetooth and Auracast and can playback mp3-stacked data discs (the go-to format for ‘mix tapes’ back in the day). Other off-kilter functions include built-in beat detection with the ability to output the tempo in sync.
The EP/BC-1 CD player is a slimline unit with pro grade features
All this is rendered in a distinctly late 80s, early 90s pro-audio aesthetic, with the red displays combined with prominent buttons and dials. Modern battery tech means the EP/BC-1 can have its own onboard rechargeable power source so it match the portability of the EP-35, while the pro audio functions make this a useful studio tool for sampling, etc.
Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1 CD player
The broadcast series promises to ‘reintroduce physical audio formats into a modern context,’ according to TE, an idea that has ‘evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.’ Perhaps we can expect something to handle vintage vinyl or even cassette tapes next. Let the format archaeology commence.
Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1 CD Player, £259, Teenage.Engineering , @TeenageEngineering

articles.title_orig: Russian threats ‘less and less hybrid,’ Von der Leyen says after assassination plot in Denmark
articles.title_zh: Russian threats ‘less and less hybrid,’ Von der Leyen says after assassination plot in Denmark
articles.content_orig:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Saturday that hybrid threats from Russia “are becoming less and less hybrid” after Danish police thwarted a plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper.
“This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable,” von der Leyen said in a statement on X on Saturday.
The Danish intelligence service, PET, announced on Friday it had averted a plot to kill the Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner, who had been due to perform in Denmark on Sept. 25.
Officials said at a press conference that a Russian intelligence service had hired two members of the Copenhagen-based gang Loyal to Familia to carry out the attack, but that police managed to stop them before it took place. The concert was then cancelled.
The suspects deny the allegations.
The Danish government reacted on Friday by expelling the Russian defense attaché , giving him seven days to leave the country.
“Moscow will respond accordingly,” Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told state-owned news agency Tass .
“The accusations against Russia are again not supported by any evidence, except for the unsubstantiated and unverifiable ‘conclusions’ and ‘data’ of Danish intelligence services,” the Russian embassy in Denmark said in a statement .
Von der Leyen said in her statement that the EU has “the tools to act” against cases like this. She said actions could range from “rapid response teams” to sanctions. She added that an upcoming European Security Strategy, which she announced in her State of the EU speech in September, could reinforce the bloc’s “preparedness and deterrence.”
It is the second time Kyivstoner has been targeted in an attempted murder plot this year. On Aug. 7 , a Russian man was detained in Poland for planning an attack against the musician, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.
Russia’s FSB security service accused the rapper in July of helping to plan drone attacks on a defense facility in the Moscow region, an allegation he denied on social media.

articles.content_orig:
While you may think quakes are a western US problem, some of the largest temblors in US history have happened in the East.
DILI, TIMOR-LESTE — A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck the Banda Sea about 65 miles northeast of Timor-Leste in Southeast Asia just after 4:30 a.m. ET (6:30 p.m. local time), according to the USGS.
MAGNITUDE 4.2 EARTHQUAKE SHAKES LOS ANGELES FOLLOWING FLURRY OF SEISMIC ACTIVITY ACROSS CENTRAL CALIFORNIA
(FOX Weather / FOX Weather)
The Southeast Asian nation shares the island of Timor with Indonesia, north of Australia .
The quake's epicenter was nearly 90 miles below the surface but was felt in the capital of Dili, as well as Darwin, Australia, some 400 miles to the southeast.
An aerial image shows the view of the city in Dili, East Timor on September 12, 2024.
((Photo by Yasuyoshi CHIBA / AFP) (Photo by YASUYOSHI CHIBA/AFP via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.
Timor-Leste sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a 25,000-mile belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean , where about 90% of the world's earthquakes occur.

articles.title_orig: There could be serious money in being a manager at your local Target or Sweetgreen
articles.title_zh: There could be serious money in being a manager at your local Target or Sweetgreen
articles.content_orig:
Early in her Target career, Brooke Pratt wondered whether shoppers mistook her for an hourly worker as she helped restock shelves.
She was actually a department manager, earning substantially more than she had in her previous job, an entry-level desk position at a public-relations firm.
"I was thinking, this isn't too bad," Pratt told Business Insider. "I'm putting cereal on the shelf, and I'm making this kind of money. It's pretty cool."
Pratt, 34, is now a store director overseeing 350 team members and 10 department managers at one of Target's largest locations, in Chaska, Minnesota.
Though a Target spokesperson said employees aren't permitted to disclose their salary, the retailer recently advertised a role in Minnesota with the same title, offering $106,000 to $212,000 in annual base pay. The spokesperson said store directors are also eligible to receive an annual bonus and stock equity.
The six-figure salaries that some managers in retail, hospitality, and other service industries now command suggest that leadership sees them as on par with their white-collar managerial counterparts. The higher pay comes at a time, though, when some tech leaders are questioning whether they need so many middle layers in the first place.
Companies including Meta and Block have been cutting their managerial ranks in recent years, arguing that layers of bosses slow decision-making. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong has said org chart layers impose a "coordination tax. "
Meanwhile, Walmart increased pay, annual stock grants, and potential bonuses last year for about 440 of its market managers, who oversee around a dozen stores. Top earners can now make as much as $620,000 in total compensation , up from about $569,000 previously.
Salad chain Sweetgreen has said it plans to introduce a 2027 total compensation plan that could pay some managers of its top-performing locations more than $200,000 a year , part of a broader retention effort.
Similar pay ranges are on offer across other labor-intensive industries. Examples include $200,000 to $300,000 for a general manager at a car dealership in Illinois and about $117,000 to $195,000 for an Apple store leader in California.
The cost of getting management wrong can be especially high in big-box retail, where managers are expected to run increasingly sophisticated operations across physical stores and online orders, said Scott Benedict, a retail consultant who worked in merchandising and e-commerce at Walmart and Sam's Club.
"There's a difference between finding a warm body and finding a leader of the caliber that you need to run what in some cases can be a $100 million or more business," he said, referring to annual sales at a single big-box location.
The pressure can also be intense at a single restaurant.
On a recent Friday morning, two online orders for 50 salads apiece came in back-to-back at a Sweetgreen in Chicago, where Ramsess Salazar, 48, oversees 26 employees who serve several hundred customers a day. With fewer people on the floor than usual, the general manager said he split his team between the digital rush and in-store guests. He then told everyone to stay calm and keep pushing.
"I have stress as well, but I cannot show it to them," Salazar said, adding that about 90 minutes later they were laughing about how many salads they had made.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Another time, a walk-in cooler broke down before lunch at a Sweetgreen in Boston, leaving Salazar with a 100-plus-salad corporate order to fill. He said he rerouted that day's delivery to a nearby sister location's cooler while a technician repaired the broken one.
The value that managers provide in consumer-facing businesses goes beyond solving crises. They often see problems and opportunities as they unfold — from a menu item that isn't selling to a staffing or service issue — and have to respond before headquarters can.
Joe de la Torre, 25, is the general manager of Crush Yard's Nashville location, a 34,000-square-foot entertainment venue offering pickleball, golf simulators, food and drinks, and other games and activities. He oversees six direct reports and 33 hourly employees, helping to run an operation that attracts between 500 and 2,000 visitors a day. De la Torre said he keeps close tabs on the facility, walking around to ensure it meets the company's standards for cleanliness, customer service, and the overall guest experience. He also sometimes helps resolve customer disputes, including disagreements among pickleball players. He then shares his observations with Crush Yard's vice president of operations.
"You get to see all fronts of the business," said de la Torre. He said he makes $84,000 a year in base salary, plus a bonus, which he estimated could bring his annual compensation to as much as $150,000.
Proximity to day-to-day operations can give service-industry managers local knowledge and influence over workers that headquarters can't easily replicate, said Raffaella Sadun, a Harvard Business School professor. In many tech companies, by contrast, leaders believe digital tools and AI can move information without a human in the middle.
That offers a lesson for white-collar managers , Sadun said: Stay close to clients and the work — and raise insights that headquarters can't see on a dashboard.
The work of a frontline manager can be decidedly unglamorous. It often means spending nearly all day on one's feet, pitching in when staffers call out, wearing a uniform, and working nights and weekends.
Pratt, the Target store director, wears tops in the retailer's signature red while on the job, and carries a walkie-talkie throughout her shift to stay in constant contact with her staff. She's also certified to use the store's powered equipment, including a forklift, and fills in for junior colleagues when needed.
"It doesn't matter really what level you are," said Pratt, who added that she learned about leadership while serving as a cheerleading team captain in college. "We all work together as a team to get something done."

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Glitch Enables First-Person POV and Open-Source App Adds 120 FPS with DLSS 5
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Glitch Enables First-Person POV and Open-Source App Adds 120 FPS with DLSS 5
articles.content_orig:
As you probably know, GTA 6 is not a game that's designed to let you freely play in first-person (at least not at launch), but thanks to some sleuthing from various GTA fans, it's been discovered that you can actually play this way.
This is thanks to a glitch that occurs when you change a specific setting and then spam the "View" button (formerly known as the "Back" button) on Xbox to trick the game into forcing you into first-person mode.
Here's how you do it (at your own risk - this is not an intended feature!):
The same instructions apply if you're on PS5, but it's the touchpad rather than the View button.
I've only been messing with this glitch a little bit so far, but it's pretty insane at first glance. You can run around, drive vehicles... do whatever you want to do. The only problem is that you can't actually back out of first-person once you're in it, although it seems some situations (like being arrested or going into a hair salon) will force you back into third-person.
So, why is Rockstar hiding this feature from us? It's probably because it's still in a work-in-progress, and there are some items that don't seem to function properly with the first-person viewpoint yet. This does seem to indicate a first-person perspective is in the works though, similar to how it was added into GTA 5 later down the line.
I'll leave you with some very, very quick screengrabs of my own down below, along with a helpful video that's getting a ton of traction on YouTube explaining how to make it work.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Down 35% From Its High. History Suggests a $5,000 Investment Now Will Be Worth This Much by 2028.
articles.content_orig:
By Keithen Drury – Nov 21, 2026 at 4:55AM EST
10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›
Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) stock has gotten slammed over the past few weeks. With former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigning from his position, the market has grown uncertain about Nvidia's future. Furthermore, some of Nvidia's practices have drawn increased scrutiny, which is also adding to fears.
After the sell-off, Nvidia is down over 35% from its all-time high. Since the AI arms race kicked off in 2023, this is now the deepest sell-off Nvidia has seen, just surpassing the tariff-fear sell-off in April 2025. The market has made its opinion known, but does Nvidia actually deserve to be sold off this much? Or is this a generational buying opportunity?
Let's take a look at where the stock could be by 2028, and if now is the perfect time to buy.
With Nvidia's sell-off, it's now down over $2 trillion from its all-time high market cap. So, is Jensen Huang really worth $2 trillion to Nvidia's market cap?
I think the market has way overblown this sell-off. Nvidia’s visionary leader definitely helped shape and drive the company. However, there are still thousands of employees who run the day-to-day operations and designs that Huang had nothing to do with. The real risk is if these employees start to quit or resign from their roles and that knowledge is lost. If there is a mass exodus from Nvidia alongside Huang, that could represent a huge risk for investors.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26
Until we're a few months past Huang's resignation, the market is likely to stay cautious, which is one reason why Nvidia's stock price is down.
Another is the future. Huang's vision for where AI computing and GPUs will go placed Nvidia in a leadership role in the AI build-out. That will have driven product development over the next couple of years, but what comes after that is unknown. This is where a new CEO will need to have a great technical mind and vision for what's coming next. The wrong person at the helm could cause Nvidia's leadership position to collapse in the future if they cannot replicate Huang’s success.
As a result, the market is once again discounting the stock until a new leader is selected.
Lastly, there are concerns that Nvidia’s chips are potentially circumventing export restrictions to China, with some restricted products funneled through Southeast Asian countries, before eventually making their way into China. These are all allegations right now, but Nvidia hasn't been cleared of any wrongdoing yet, so once again, the market is discounting the stock.
Nvidia has a lot of unknowns right now, and the market has kept it in a low-valued spot as a result. The question is, if these are resolved, what could it be worth?
Nvidia has guided for 75% revenue growth in fiscal year (FY) 2028 (ending January 2028), thanks to the strength of the AI build-out. That's up from the 70% guidance given last quarter. With Nvidia estimated to generate around $424 billion in revenue this year, that would indicate revenue of $742 billion next year. At Nvidia's 62% profit margin, the company would generate $460 billion in profits.
Even if the stock traded at the same trailing earnings multiple it does now, that would give it a market cap of $7.4 trillion -- more than doubling today's levels and turning $5,000 into at least $10,000.
NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts
However, I think that is a dirt cheap price tag in and of itself, and most of Nvidia's problems will be solved by the end of next year. As a result, the market could value it like any other big tech stock and price it around 20 to 25 times earnings. That would result in an even larger market cap and make Nvidia a no-brainer buy today.

articles.title_orig: UK maritime agency reports two tanker incidents near Oman; Iran says vessel hit mine east of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: UK maritime agency reports two tanker incidents near Oman; Iran says vessel hit mine east of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.title_zh: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street suffers historic losses as Dow, S&P 500 plunge into correction territory
articles.title_zh: Wall Street suffers historic losses as Dow, S&P 500 plunge into correction territory
articles.content_orig:
FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis has the latest on the massive sell-off in the U.S. stock market amid a widespread artificial intelligence stock sell-off on 'Special Report.'
U.S. stocks plunged Friday in one of Wall Street's worst trading sessions in years, when a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence companies wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the year and pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory.
The historic sell-off sent major U.S. indexes sharply lower, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling nearly 950 points, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.28%.
Both the Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from their recent record highs.
The steep decline erased the Nasdaq's gains for the year, marking its second-largest single-day point drop on record.
ANTHROPIC'S $1.5 TRILLION IPO SETS OFF A FRESH WAVE OF TECH WEALTH HEADING FOR SOUTH FLORIDA
U.S. stocks plunged Friday in one of Wall Street's worst trading sessions in years as a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence companies sent major indexes sharply lower. (Reuters/Brendan McDermid / Reuters)
"It was a brutal day in the stock market with AI fears taking center stage," FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis reported Friday on "Special Report."
Investors directed much of their selling toward technology companies, putting additional pressure on the Nasdaq, Willis noted.
"Investors saved their real wrath for the tech-heavy Nasdaq," Willis said.
The massive sell-off came amid mounting concerns about the AI boom, with some of the industry's biggest names suffering steep losses, including chip-making giant Nvidia and newly public AI developer Anthropic.
HOLIDAY AIRFARES HIT HIGHEST LEVELS IN A DECADE AS JET FUEL PRICES SURGE
Wall Street suffered steep losses Friday as concerns over artificial intelligence stocks wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the year and pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Nvidia shares tumbled approximately 14%, while Anthropic fell about 9% during its second trading session as a public company.
Friday's declines came despite strong earnings from Nvidia and a highly anticipated stock market debut for Anthropic, which failed to ease investor concerns about soaring AI valuations and spending.
Recent technology disruptions affecting major companies and institutions over the past 10 days may have contributed to investor unease, Willis said.
"Much of the investor anxiety [has been] spiking this week on reports of tech meltdowns at companies as diverse as United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase," Willis said.
ANTHROPIC IPO TURNS THOUSANDS OF TECH WORKERS INTO OVERNIGHT MILLIONAIRES, REPORTS SAY
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks Thursday during its initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters / Reuters)
The historic losses capped a particularly difficult week for Wall Street , with the S&P 500 posting its worst weekly percentage decline since April 2025, while the Nasdaq recorded its largest weekly percentage loss since March 2020.
The Dow also suffered its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, according to Reuters.
Friday marked the S&P 500's seventh consecutive losing session, its longest losing streak since February 2020.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 950 points Friday as Wall Street suffered a broad sell-off driven by weakness in technology stocks. (Yuki Iwamura/AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The market turmoil also sent Wall Street's closely watched volatility index, commonly known as the VIX or "fear gauge," to its highest closing level since April 2025.

Willis also noted that gold prices rose as investors sought safer assets amid the sell-off.

articles.title_orig: Japan wary of U.S., Russia and China holding regular summits
articles.title_zh: Japan wary of U.S., Russia and China holding regular summits
articles.content_orig:
After the United States, China and Russia held an unprecedented trilateral summit on Thursday, Japan is concerned that the trilateral framework may become a regular occurrence.
On the heels of the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held telephone talks with Trump to affirm close cooperation between Japan and the United States.
At a news conference in Tokyo on Friday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara stressed, “We’ll communicate closely with our allies and like-minded nations and work to maintain and strengthen a free and open international order.”
Japan is eager to maintain the existing international order, including by strengthening the rule of law.
In a joint peace declaration released after the summit, the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders confirmed their commitment to “maintaining strategic stability and international security.” A Japanese government official said, “We were relieved that nothing major was decided at the summit.”
Still, there are concerns in Japan that the three major powers may hold summits on a regular basis. A senior Foreign Ministry official said, “That all depends on how serious Trump is (about the three-way framework).”
At a U.S.-China summit in September, Trump noted that the two countries were allies during World War II. At Thursday’s meeting, Xi said that the three nations fought side by side in the war against fascism, and Putin said that their shared victory in the war united them.
“We cannot overlook the fact that China and Russia are bringing up such ties,” said a high-ranking Japanese government official.
The peace declaration also warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The ICC, based in The Hague in the Netherlands, has issued an arrest warrant for Putin over his country’s invasion of Ukraine, and has launched an investigation into alleged war crimes by U.S. military personnel.
As Japan supports the ICC, headed by Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, the disagreement between Tokyo and Washington over the court may become a source of friction.
Speaking to reporters after the phone talks with Trump on Thursday evening, Takaichi admitted that Japan and the United States have different views. However, she stressed, “Japan’s position is to strengthen the rule of law while cooperating with relevant countries.”
In her message to an international conference on Ukraine held the same day, Takaichi said that any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force must not be tolerated.

articles.title_zh: Capricor's Duchenne treatment fails to get FDA approval, shares sink
articles.content_orig:
Adam Feuerstein, a senior writer and biotech columnist, is the author of Adam’s Biotech Scorecard , a subscriber-only newsletter about the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology.
Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. He is also a co-host of the weekly biotech podcast The Readout Loud and author of the newsletter Adam’s Biotech Scorecard. You can reach Adam on Signal at stataf.54.
The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.
The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials . Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.
But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths and physics .
A group of maths scholars said AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title_orig: Trump signs Common Cents Act into law
articles.title_zh: Trump signs Common Cents Act into law
articles.content_orig:
Washington is officially done with spending a pretty penny on penny production .
President Donald Trump on Friday signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act , which formally directs the federal government to stop minting the penny.
Both the House and the Senate passed the measure by voice vote, meaning no notable opposition.
“It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny,” the bill’s author, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Sept. 29 on X a day after Senate passage . “This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it’s common sense!”
The U.S. Mint last year put the immediate annual savings of discontinuing penny production at $56 million .
The government stopped making pennies in November 2025 , nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production , writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” However, the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector versions to be produced in “limited quantities.”
The penny can still be used as legal tender “for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues,” according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence “for as long as possible.”
The new measure also provides a procedure for stores and businesses that accept cash payments to round their prices to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents.
And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint’s currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.
Congress passed the Coinage Act in 1792, and the U.S. Mint began producing the penny, known officially as the cent, the following year.
In its nearly 250 years in production, the penny has had multiple facades. It wasn’t until 1909 that it was given its modern-day face, featuring President Abraham Lincoln.
The first penny, produced in 1787, had a sundial design created by Benjamin Franklin. After the U.S. Mint took over, the penny was slightly bigger and included the image of a woman representing Liberty on one side and 15 chain links on the other.
The next penny debuted in 1857, taking on a smaller shape and displaying a flying eagle design on one side and a wreath on the other. It also changed from being 100% copper to 88% copper and 12% nickel. Two years later, an “Indian Head” design was added to one side.
The most recent design from the U.S. Mint was issued in 2010, featuring its “Union Shield” theme. It shows a shield on the tails side of the coin to represent “Lincoln’s preservation of the United States as a single country,” the U.S. Mint wrote.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: House Lawmakers Push US AI Models to Counter China
articles.title_zh: House Lawmakers Push US AI Models to Counter China
articles.content_orig:
United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls.
This week, the US Department of Commerce announced a new rule to restrict how advanced US AI chips can be accessed remotely in the wake of the previous Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected spy for Beijing. The move would close what officials described as a loophole that allows Chinese companies to tap into computing power through data centres in third countries, bypassing US restrictions.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which sits under the Commerce Department, said the rule would require data centre customers in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy advanced chips from US companies, including Nvidia, because they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.
“The export controls should have been in place, certainly,” Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal told Al Jazeera. “I also think it’s a bigger conversation about who dominates the AI market. We should not have this consolidation of all the AI knowledge in a couple of companies because that poses an enormous threat on multiple levels, including national security.”
In October, Jayapal introduced a policy framework that would require every AI company operating in the US to obtain a federal charter in an effort to protect the public interest.
The AI charter, the framework says, is modelled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons.
The framework also bans AI companies from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm.
Jayapal is a member of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, whose ranking members announced a probe to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.
Lutnick is facing criticism, including from members of US President Donald Trump’s cabinet, for allegedly refusing to impose restrictions on companies accused of diverting advanced chips to China, including Megaspeed, which is at the centre of the Nvidia probe.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee also announced that the Trump administration had approved exports of 879,000 chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026.
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, expressed a desire to better limit chip exports amid growing scrutiny over the extent to which US computing power may have reached China.
“I’m excited to get these gavels and go through the investigatory work that’s necessary, but also to rein in and regulate artificial intelligence. The very industry is asking to be regulated by Congress,” Democratic Representative Everton Blair told Al Jazeera.
The US accounts for nearly 75 percent of the world’s AI spending and computing power, followed by China.
US tech giants, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, operate nearly 90 major AI computing hubs globally, according to an Oxford University study. The same research found that US companies were building 63 AI computing hubs outside the country as of 2025.
Stephen Ezell, vice president for global innovation policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), said Washington would find it difficult to enforce the BIS rule.
China has rejected the restriction, calling it “economic coercion” by the US.
On Friday, after his return to the White House from his historic trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian presidents in Shenzhen, China, Trump promised to prohibit US companies from developing data centres in other countries.
“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” Trump said.
It was unclear what Trump had envisioned, or how he would enforce it.
At the same time, he urged Americans to embrace data centres in their neighbourhoods, despite communities’ increasing concern about the centres’ impact on quality of life, environment and energy demands.
Analysts say the recent export regulation has likely not had much effect on China’s efforts to become the global leader in AI semiconductor chips.
“China does not want to depend upon American or other foreign semiconductors. They want to develop them themselves, and one can argue that we’ve slowed them down a little bit with our export controls, but in no way has it changed China’s aspirations to become the global AI semiconductor chip leader,” Ezell said on Al Jazeera’s This Is America .

articles.title_orig: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on Friday accused President Donald Trump of putting US national security at risk by allowing advanced artificial intelligence chips to be exported to Chinese companies, including those with alleged ties to China's military.
Speaking on the Senate floor, Schumer cited information released by the House of Representatives showing that the Trump administration approved nearly 900,000 shipments of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies during the first six months after easing export restrictions.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday disclosed that the Commerce Department approved 879,000 shipments of advanced Nvidia and AMD chips between December 2025 and May 2026.
The shipments included 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all of which the Pentagon lists as companies allegedly linked to the Chinese military, according to the House committee.
Schumer alleged that the Commerce Department authorized the sale of tens of thousands of Nvidia chips to a company affiliated with a Chinese intelligence operative who had previously targeted former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Last week, Huang resigned after 33 years as CEO, following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick knew about the woman's alleged intelligence ties before the sales were approved, according to Schumer.
"Keep in mind, Trump and Lutnick knew this woman was a spy ahead of time, and still rushed to approve the sale of this sensitive technology to her companies," he said.
"Trump and Lutnick sold out America's national security to make a quick buck for themselves and their billionaire buddies," said Schumer, accusing the administration of prioritizing financial interests over US security and technological competitiveness.
The Democratic leader also criticized Trump's reception this week by Chinese officials, arguing that Beijing's warm welcome was connected to the administration's decision to loosen restrictions on advanced American semiconductor exports.
"Trump needs to realize that the only reason he received such a warm welcome from the Chinese Communist Party this week was because he's doling out our most advanced AI chips to China, like their party favors," he said.
Schumer urged Congress to pass three pieces of legislation to tighten oversight of AI chip exports: the AI Overwatch Act, the MATCH Act, and the Chips Security Act.
Schumer is seeking the post of Senate majority leader in the new Congress starting in January, in which Democrats are set to enjoy a 56-44 Senate majority over Republicans. One senator, Chris Van Hollen, is challenging Schumer for the job.
Democrats have pledged to carry out more vigorous oversight of the Trump administration once they take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate on Jan. 3.

articles.title_orig: Fresh off China Trip, Trump Bobs and Weaves in Freewheeling Press Conference
articles.title_zh: Fresh off China Trip, Trump Bobs and Weaves in Freewheeling Press Conference
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
articles.title_zh: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
articles.content_orig:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title_orig: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
articles.title_zh: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump ’s warm greeting for Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China Thursday sparked concern and ire from some European lawmakers.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to mock Trump’s labeling of Putin as “ my friend ” with a pointed social media message that read : “God, protect us from such friends.”
The post was shared just hours before Tusk headed to a meeting in Berlin of the “ Coalition of the Willing ,” an initiative intended to bolster support for Ukraine more than four years after its invasion by Russia. Tusk joined leaders from Germany, France, Britain, and Italy, along with NATO chief Mark Rutte and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Also in attendance were U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who briefed the group on Trump’s meetings with Putin in China. The session saw Europe secure a seat at the negotiating table for the next stage of U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Tusk, meanwhile, made another apparent dig at Trump during the meeting as he posted a picture of himself sharing a laugh with Zelensky and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside the caption: "True friendship."
Further critique came from Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who reportedly told the media: “The optics of this cosying up to Putin—calling him a 'friend'—cause us some concern, because it raises the question: with whom is he truly friends?”
Trump hailed his "great relationship" with Putin ahead of their historic trilateral sit-down with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Addressing Ukraine at the top of the meeting, Trump said: "I think things are happening. I think that he [Putin] and—I hope—the other side would like to see an end to that war.” However, the China-U.S.-Russia “peace declaration” published by Chinese state media after the trilateral summit notably included no mention of Ukraine.
European leaders vowed to support Ukraine "for as long as it takes" at the close of the session in Berlin.
Emphasizing the need for Europe to be involved in talks moving forward, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters: "Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A 'Yalta-style' format will not bring about peace.”
With negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators have sought to instead steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction. In line with this, Kushner told reporters that the U.S. is open to giving Ukraine NATO-like security guarantees.
"I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that," he said, before going on to claim that Russia is “comfortable” with the idea, also.
Kushner added that Trump had called into the meeting to join the discussions with European leaders.
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelensky celebrated the assured inclusion of Europe in future negotiations, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements.
"Europe will be represented by five countries plus the European Union and NATO, and America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation in the negotiations is necessary," he said .
The wartime leader went on to express the need for progress to be made ahead of Ukraine being plunged into its fifth winter at-war.
"We must take the necessary steps to ensure that Russia engages in serious, substantive work instead of wasting time. This is very important to us because people are dying—our Ukrainians," he urged. "Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia."
Donald Tusk, Andy Burnham, Volodymyr Zelensky, Friedrich Merz, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, and Bart De Wever are seated at the "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. Kay Nietfeld—AP
While European leaders have banded together to place further sanctions on Russia, in a bid to ramp up economic pressure on the Kremlin to end the war, there has been growing concern over Trump’s approach to Putin.
Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia in order to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.
Amid the deal, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets. Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a " disgrace " and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than Putin."
After meeting with Putin in Russia last week, Witkoff told reporters that he thought "progress" had been made, but Russia and Ukraine have traded strikes in the days since. The sit-down in Moscow came after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.
Meanwhile, the European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday that ministers had approved new listings to target Russian refineries, banks, e-commerce, and companies that support Russia’s shadow fleet, a network of vessels that help Moscow evade sanctions on energy exports. Kallas added that the 22nd sanctions package against Russia would be presented in-full within the next few days.
The united response and continued economic pressure from Europe stands in stark contrast to how the Trump Administration is currently dealing with Putin.
Further tensions between Europe and Washington have stemmed from the early days of the Iran war, after European leaders refused to actively get involved in the conflict—earning public rebuke from Trump. The global energy crisis that has since ensued, and the soaring fuel costs, has also soured relations. Other topics of contention include NATO spending and tariff rows .
The Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections earlier this month were viewed by some European leaders as a rebuke of Trump and his Administration’s policies. “American society voted against policies that only make people poorer. Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege,” said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has previously clashed with Trump .
